items.title: Texas’ School Voucher Program Could Be “Unrecognizable, If Not Extinct,” Says Democratic Lawmaker
items.abstract: The post Texas’ School Voucher Program Could Be “Unrecognizable, If Not Extinct,” Says Democratic Lawmaker appeared first on ProPublica .
paras: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s vision for education was finally coming together.

This year, the state launched a voucher program that allowed roughly 110,000 of Texas’ more than 5 million schoolchildren to get a private education using taxpayer dollars. Abbott’s loyal appointee at the Texas Education Agency, Commissioner Mike Morath, was leading the state’s largest takeover of public schools in recent history . And the Texas State Board of Education, with Abbott’s support , helped pass a controversial new social studies curriculum that required teaching Bible stories and shifted away from world history to focus on Texas and the United States.
On Tuesday night, as Democrats clinched nearly every office in the state, it all began to unravel.
In a speech after denying Abbott a fourth term, Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa called for a reversal of his education agenda. She pledged to fire Morath and to end the public school takeovers.
Perhaps most significantly, she doubled down on a campaign promise to erase one of Abbott’s biggest accomplishments: school vouchers.
“We will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam,” said Hinojosa, who did not respond to requests for an interview.
It is not clear how Hinojosa will deliver on that promise. While Democrats have the ability to restrict parts of the program, eliminating it would require legislative action.
But Hinojosa will have help.

Democrat Sarah Eckhardt, a former state senator who voted against vouchers and will now lead the state office charged with running the program, has said she will push changes to increase accountability and transparency.
Eckhardt, however, acknowledged the limitations of her office, saying that any big overhaul must come from lawmakers.
Democrats won back the Texas House for the first time in 24 years, but Republicans retained a majority in the Senate.
Rep. Diego Bernal, the Democratic vice chair of the House education committee, seemed confident that there is a path toward killing the program, at least as it now exists.

Bernal, whose district is in San Antonio, said some Republican colleagues previously told him privately that they had reservations about the voucher program, but were limited in what they could do because of pressure from leaders who have now been ousted.
“I guarantee that program is not going to be untouched, and it will be probably unrecognizable, if not extinct, by the time we’re done with it,” he said.

Abbott spent years trying to pass a statewide voucher program. By 2024, he’d grown angry at rural Republicans who repeatedly blocked such legislation because, they argued, public schools were a vital part of their communities. So Abbott shelled out millions of dollars to oust them from office and elect pro-voucher Republicans instead.

He succeeded. And the following year, those Republicans helped pass the $1 billion state voucher program. This week, at least 13 Republicans who Abbott had previously endorsed or helped fund as part of his voucher push lost to Democrats or were trailing in close races.
Abbott’s office declined an interview request, referring ProPublica and The Texas Tribune to his campaign office, which did not respond.
His bullishness on vouchers turned off some Republican voters in rural communities that have historically been strongholds for his party, education experts and politicians said.

A Texas Tribune analysis found Democrats made striking gains in rural and semirural parts of the state , where concern over vouchers, along with issues like data centers, ran high. In rural counties, Abbott’s margin over Hinojosa fell 16 percentage points from his 2022 margin over former U.S. Rep. Beto O’Rourke, and it fell 20 percentage points in exurban counties.

Former state Rep. Dewayne Burns, an anti-voucher Republican from a mostly rural district south of Fort Worth who was defeated by an Abbott-backed primary challenger in 2024, said many of his constituents felt betrayed by the governor’s push for vouchers. “That’s the first time that I think rural Texans really kind of stepped back and said, ‘Are you guys really supporting us?’” he said. “I think they overestimated the loyalty that Texans, especially rural Texans, had to the governor.”

Former state Rep. Steve Allison, who represented a suburban San Antonio district before he was unseated in the 2024 primary, said he remains convinced his constituents never wanted the voucher system. Pro-voucher groups targeted him in a series of ads that attacked him for issues like border security and property taxes but said little about school choice. Polls at the time showed Texans held complicated views on school choice, with one University of Houston poll showing that while two-thirds of Texans supported voucher legislation, an equal number believed that vouchers would funnel money away from already struggling public schools.

“I know what I saw when my staff took very careful notice of what phone calls were coming in and what emails and texts and visits were coming in,” he said in an interview. “It was clear that the overall district was opposed to vouchers.”

Concerns about vouchers became key in several rural and suburban Texas districts this year where Abbott’s selected candidates had won two years ago. One of those races was for Allison’s old seat, which pro-voucher candidate Marc LaHood won in 2024 after Abbott spent at least $700,000 supporting him.

Another was in Bell County in Central Texas. There, the Abbott-backed incumbent, Rep. Hillary Hickland, conceded a close race Wednesday morning. She did not respond to a request for an interview. Her Democratic opponent, Amelia Rabroker, a former teacher, said the Republicans’ heavy-handed push for vouchers spurred her to challenge Hickland.

“A lot of money was pushed into her campaign to make that happen, and she delivered on those vouchers, and it was very upsetting to the people of Central Texas,” Rabroker said. “I think it was a huge concern. The biggest.”

Similarly, LaHood, who did not respond to requests for comment, faced a flurry of questions over his support of vouchers at a candidate forum for the District 121 race in October. His opponent, Democrat Zack Dunn, said vouchers and public education were second only to affordability in the minds of voters he met. On Tuesday night, Dunn defeated LaHood with 54% of vote.

“Across the board, overwhelmingly the sentiment was, ‘We need to fully fund our public schools,’” Dunn said in an interview. “The voucher scam, the voucher scheme, the voucher vote that was taken is hurting us. It’s hurting us definitely across the state, but it’s hurting us in 121. Yes, we heard that over and over and over again.”
Dunn said he would support measures that ensure more transparency in how taxpayer dollars are used for private schools.
Ultimately, though, he wants to see the program repealed.

Some changes can come through administrative actions by Eckhardt, the new state comptroller. In a news conference the day after her election, Eckhardt said she planned to rigorously audit how taxpayer money is spent and to release more information about the program to the public.

Under her Republican predecessors, the comptroller’s office shielded information that included data detailing how much state funding certain private schools received and how many students most public schools lost to the program. The office argued that it was protecting student privacy.

“As the comptroller, my job is to vigorously follow the money and report back to the Legislature if their investment is not panning out,” Eckhardt said. She added, “That is part of the vigorous audit and performance evaluation of this program that any comptroller should be doing, and I certainly will be doing.”
One key supporter of vouchers in the Senate, the last Republican bulwark in the state, is taking a more measured approach on the program’s future.

Houston Republican Sen. Paul Bettencourt, who led the effort to approve vouchers that had failed in prior years, said the Legislature will need to review the outcomes from the 2026-27 school year and assess the benefits and families’ concerns. He pointed to the fact that vouchers were returned by some parents whose children required special education services.

“I think that it has helped students in many other states,” Bettencourt said. “We need to look at what’s happened here with this first cohort, and we need to make sure that we’re debating not the emotionality prior to passage of a bill, but the facts of what happened after the passage of a bill.”

Scott Schneider, an attorney who represents private schools participating in the voucher program, said the midterm results shocked private school leaders. Some were counting on the state funding to support their business. He said private school leaders could start a lobbying effort to grandfather in the families already benefiting from the program, but schools are also planning for what they will do if the state funding goes away altogether.
“It’s going to be a hot mess,” Schneider said.

items.title: How people in Montenegro are making their country cleaner
items.abstract: While Montenegro works to align its waste management with EU directives, ordinary citizens are taking practical steps to improve the situation now.
paras: And helping to make the goals for EU accession plausible
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from the EkoMapa website of the EkoGard organization in Montenegro. Fair use.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup , in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Montenegro is on its way to joining the EU; at the moment, the goal is to do so by 2028. The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe ( UNECE) review in 2025 states that the country has made significant progress in aligning its environmental legal and regulatory framework, as well as much of its national legislation, with European Union (EU) directives.
However, some problems remain, including waste management and a very low recycling rate — less than 2 percent, far below the EU’s 50 percent target .

Austrian Member of Parliament Thomas Waitz (Greens/EFA), chair of the delegation to the EU-Montenegro Stabilisation and Association Parliamentary Committee, said in an interview with The New Union Post that there have been “massive improvements” in Montenegro, citing as an example the closure of more than 100 illegal landfills in the last year: “It is a great effort for such a small country. But they have another 500, and if we expected them to have them all cleaned up, it would be impossible.”

While politicians and international agencies discuss how Montenegro could get closer to the target and put its waste management under control, ordinary citizens are making practical steps to improve the situation today.
This Digital Spark spotlight story is about one such organization, EkoGard , and the many people who participate in its efforts and, step by step, try to make Montenegro cleaner.
Global Voices interviewed the organization’s founder and general director, Senad Pepić, about the impact of Digital Spark and its community initiative.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.

Senad Pepić (SP): EkoGard was built through years of work on the ground, not in an office. It grew out of the Očistimo Rožaje initiative , where we spent six years building a strong community of people ready to take action. We started with illegal dumpsites, but our work gradually expanded to other environmental and social issues affecting everyday life.
We organized cleanups, worked with young people, launched campaigns, and encouraged residents to tackle problems that kept coming back.

We joined Digital Spark because we wanted to bring what we learned in the field together with digital tools and data. We hoped to show a fuller picture of the problems and change how people talk about them. EkoMapa grew out of that idea as a natural next step in our work.
GV: What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

SP : One cleanup in particular made us rethink our approach. We cleared an illegal dumpsite beside a rural road, in an area where residents had no suitable place to dispose of their waste. The nearest legal disposal point was about six kilometers away.

After the cleanup, we asked for a waste container to be installed and were promised that the problem would be addressed. Three years passed; the container was never installed, and the dumpsite returned.

Its return changed how we saw similar sites elsewhere. We had photos, posts, and letters from other areas, but no way to see the full extent of the problem or how it related to gaps in waste collection services.

We wanted to map these places and understand the conditions in each settlement. Doing that gives us a way to show local institutions where waste disposal services are lacking and talk about what needs to change.
GV: What are the key changes or activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

SP : Before this project, EkoGard organized cleanups, worked with young people, held educational activities, ran campaigns, and drew attention to local problems. Through Digital Spark, we began collecting and analysing what we saw in the field more systematically.

EkoMapa started as a map of illegal dumpsites , but it grew into a tool for understanding environmental conditions across the community. We decided to look at conditions settlement by settlement, so we could connect the problems we found with the services available to residents.

We also developed a model that uses the information we collect to assess environmental risks and gaps in local services in each settlement. It helps us spot patterns, compare needs across settlements, and discuss what the data shows with local institutions.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.
SP : Our activists now have a practical tool and a clearer way to document what they find. We can use that information in public campaigns and make a stronger case for change.
For residents, we can now show how the problems they face relate to the services available in their settlements.
Organizations from other towns and countries have also shown interest in using the tool to understand conditions in their own communities and involve residents in finding solutions.

The local waste management company has also recognized that the information could be useful in its work. For now, the clearest changes are in how our activists work and in the conversations we have begun with other organizations and local institutions. Changes on the ground will take longer.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

SP : Through the project, we learned that giving people a way to report a problem is only a first step. They also need to know why we collect the information, what we will do with it, and how it might lead to change.
The training on how to reach people and communicate more clearly was especially useful. It made us think about the words we use and how to talk about problems without making people feel powerless.

For us, digital democracy means residents can help identify problems and take part in finding solutions. When we collect, check, and present what they tell us clearly, it can inform our campaigns and conversations with institutions. It also helps us ask for clearer answers.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

SP: The most valuable lesson is that technology cannot solve a problem on its own. It can help us see what is happening across a community, but it cannot replace fieldwork, talking with residents, or working with institutions.
Finding a problem on a map is just the beginning. We also need to understand why it happened. If we only deal with what we can see, the same problem is likely to return.

When we bring the data together with people’s experiences, we can start to propose solutions that meet their needs. That is what we will take into our future work: listen, look for patterns and causes, and use what we learn to push for change.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

SP: Our next step is to present our findings to the local government and make the case for better planning of waste collection and other local services. We want to draw attention to settlements that have been overlooked for years and follow up on how institutions respond.

We are already applying what we learned to EkoGard’s wider work, especially our campaigns and how we involve residents. Together with other organizations from Montenegro, we are preparing a campaign to establish a National Eco Line, a nationwide channel for reporting environmental problems and following up on how the responsible authorities respond.
We know the results may take time, so we will keep working with other organizations and local institutions.

items.title: Big Tech, AI, and the quiet expansion of digital surveillance in Nigeria
items.abstract: ...systems designed to maximise commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.
paras: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
Originally published on Global Voices
Illustration by Nshua Cali-Dibang, used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “ Big Tech and Authoritarianism .” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here .

Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user. Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant. Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, technology companies are finding new ways to use data to develop their products, personalize services and generate revenue. While these developments offer considerable benefits, they also raise a difficult question: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?

The issue extends beyond privacy policies and user agreements. It concerns the growing power of technology companies to collect information, draw conclusions about individuals, and influence the digital environments in which people communicate, work, and access information.

In September 2024, the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published findings from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch.

The FTC reported that these companies collected extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users. The information included personal details, interests, online activities, and data obtained from other sources. The investigation also raised concerns about lengthy data retention, inadequate privacy protections, and the use of personal information in automated systems, including AI.

The report highlighted a fundamental imbalance: Companies can accumulate substantial information about individuals, while those individuals may have limited understanding of how their data is used or how to prevent certain uses.

AI adds another dimension to this problem. Data can help train models, improve recommendations, and power automated decisions. However, the greater the volume and variety of information companies can access, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on its collection and use.

The concern is not that every company collecting data is necessarily acting maliciously. Rather, it is that systems designed to maximize commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.

For millions of people, AI offers opportunities that were previously difficult to access. Students can use AI tools to support learning, small businesses can improve their operations, and journalists can explore new approaches to research and production.

In countries such as Nigeria, where access to resources and professional services can be uneven, these tools could help narrow certain gaps. AI systems that support local languages and reflect diverse cultural experiences could also make digital services more accessible.

Yet inclusion should mean more than allowing people to use a technology. It should also mean ensuring that they understand the conditions under which they use it and retain meaningful rights over their information.

Many digital services are governed by lengthy terms and privacy policies that users may accept without fully understanding the implications. Some AI products also raise questions about whether information submitted through prompts, uploaded documents, or other interactions may be retained or used to improve models.

The precise practices differ between companies and products. Nevertheless, users need clear explanations of what information is collected, why it is needed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for purposes beyond the immediate service.
Without these safeguards, the benefits of AI inclusion risk coming with an invisible cost: reduced control over personal information.

The connection between big tech and authoritarianism requires careful examination. Authoritarianism is not simply the collection of data by private companies. It involves the concentration and exercise of power in ways that undermine accountability, rights, and freedoms.

However, extensive corporate data collection can create conditions that make surveillance easier. Detailed personal information can support profiling, targeted persuasion and the prediction of individual behavior. Depending on the circumstances, businesses, governments, or other actors may exploit these capabilities.

The risks become particularly serious when personal data can be accessed or shared without adequate safeguards, when automated systems make consequential decisions without meaningful oversight, or when people have little opportunity to challenge how their information is used.

Concentrated corporate power adds another concern. When a small number of companies control widely used digital platforms, AI services, and large pools of information, individuals may have few practical alternatives. Leaving a platform may mean losing access to professional networks, customers, communities, or essential services.

This does not mean that every AI system is a surveillance tool or that every technology company intends to restrict freedom. It means that the infrastructure of digital life deserves scrutiny because its capabilities can be used in ways that extend beyond their original commercial purpose.

Nigeria has a legal framework intended to protect individuals against the misuse of their personal information. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and provides a framework for the lawful, fair and accountable processing of personal data.
Legislation is an important step, but effective protection also depends on implementation, public awareness, and regulators’ ability to hold organizations accountable.

As Nigerians increasingly adopt AI-powered services, questions about data governance become more pressing. Users need to understand their rights, while organizations must take responsibility for explaining their practices and protecting the information they collect.

There is also a wider question of representation. If AI systems are developed using data that inadequately reflects Nigerian languages, cultures, and social realities, their benefits may be distributed unevenly. Responsible AI governance must therefore address both the protection of personal information and the inclusion of communities whose experiences are often underrepresented.

UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence emphasizes privacy, data protection, transparency, accountability, and fairness throughout the AI lifecycle. These principles provide a useful foundation for ensuring that technological progress respects human rights.

The challenge is not to reject AI or prevent companies from using data to develop useful technologies. It is to establish boundaries that allow innovation without making personal privacy an acceptable casualty.

Technology companies should minimize unnecessary data collection, communicate their policies clearly, provide meaningful choices, and strengthen protections against unauthorized access. Regulators must ensure that existing laws remain effective as AI capabilities evolve, while users need accessible information about the rights available to them.

Ultimately, digital inclusion cannot be measured solely by the number of people using AI. It must also consider whether those people can participate safely, understand the systems they rely on, and exercise meaningful control over their information.

As AI becomes more powerful, the question is no longer simply what technology can do with our data. It is who decides what can be done, who benefits from those decisions, and who has the power to challenge them.
The future of AI should not be defined only by what machines learn about us, but also by how much control we retain over ourselves.

items.title: Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest
items.abstract: Pope Leo’s November 2026 trip to Latin America will bring him back to Peru, where he served as a priest and bishop for two decades.
paras: Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship.
As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America.

Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru . He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital. In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has drastically cut funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people.

And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero. A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero was assassinated in 1980 after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the U.S.-supported Salvadoran military . His ministry was influenced by liberation theology , a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru.
What is liberation theology?
The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutiérrez , a Peruvian theologian and priest. He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “ A Theology of Liberation .”

Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty to liberate the oppressed . They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins. While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism.

Catholics inspired by liberation theology created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor. In my own research , I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives.

Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about analyzing society and the economy to better understand inequality . In nations like Peru, which possessed rich natural resources , liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers.
During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism.

A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism. Christians for Socialism , for example, argued that liberation meant rejecting capitalism . Some clergy, although only a handful, even picked up arms to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups.
A wary pope
This presented a dilemma to the Vatican.

In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – the current pope’s namesake – published “Rerum Novarum ,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution. Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies.

During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics , including some in Chulucanas, Peru , where Leo began his missionary work. Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression.

But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978. For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion. A staunch opponent of communism , he worried about liberation theology’s use of Marxist analysis. So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI.

The Vatican began investigating some liberation theologians for violations of church teachings. In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a year of silence – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy. Several priests were suspended over their work in Sandinista Nicaragua.
John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over Marxism’s influence on his work . Gutiérrez was ultimately not punished.

One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s. The Shining Path , a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru.

Under President Alberto Fujimori, the government escalated existing counterinsurgency operations, often using indiscriminate violence against citizens in the region where the Shining Path emerged. In 2009, Fujimori was convicted of human rights violations .
Young priest

Leo has never described himself as a liberationist Catholic. However, his experiences as a priest were indelibly shaped by liberation theology , the Peruvian armed conflict and the church debates that roiled much of Latin America during his years there.

Leo, born Robert Prevost, was raised in Chicago. After ordination, his journey as a priest began in Peru, where he landed for missionary work in 1985. The young friar followed in the footsteps of other U.S. Catholic missionaries who had been serving among Peru’s poor and Indigenous, urban and rural, since the 1940s.

Sent to Chulucanas, in Peru’s coastal northwest, Prevost found himself in a region of pastoral experimentation. Since the 1960s, Augustinian missionaries had been working closely with the community to provide literacy education, discussion groups about poverty and inequality, and workshops to train artisans.

These programs were a far cry from the more radical actions of some Catholics who supported liberation theology. Nevertheless, the programs in Chulucanas aimed to empower the Peruvian poor, chipping away at exploitation and low wages on the region’s sugarcane and cotton estates. Like Gutiérrez, many Peruvian Christians believed that the Shining Path drew support because of pervasive poverty and inequality , and that churches could help transform the nation.

But the Catholic Church in Latin America was in the midst of another transformation. John Paul gradually appointed conservative bishops across the continent. Experimental pastoral programs lost support, and institutions that trained priests to put liberation theology into action, such as the Regional Seminary of the Southeast in Mexico, were shuttered or “reoriented.”

Yet even as the hierarchy shifted conservative, work on the ground among Latin America’s poorest continued apace. From coffee cooperatives in Mexico to human rights activists across the continent, many programs survived.
‘Cease the repression’

Leo’s 2026 itinerary includes multiple stops that speak to this history and on-the-ground pastoral work. The most symbolic, perhaps, is the Capilla San Óscar Romero, located in Chiclayo, the pope’s former diocese.

A neighborhood chapel renovated with donations from Leo’s connections in the United States, it is one of many sites throughout the Americas honoring Catholics who fell victim to right-wing, anti-communist violence. The day before Romero’s assassination, he used his weekly radio address to speak directly to El Salvador’s conscripted soldiers, telling them, “ No soldier is obliged to obey an order counter to the law of God .”

Leo XIV’s visit to the chapel is for private prayer, not a homily or a speech. Still, I would argue that the soft-spoken pope’s stop will evoke Romero’s message – especially at a time of strikes against suspected drug traffickers , which human rights groups have criticized as extrajudicial killings . During his final Mass , Romero pleaded, “I beseech you, I beg you, I command you in the name of God: Cease the repression!”

items.title: On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm Debacle
items.abstract: The post On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm Debacle appeared first on ProPublica .
paras: Jacob Hawk leaned over the plastic fencing to get Vivek Ramaswamy’s attention as the Republican candidate for Ohio governor moved down the line shaking hands at the Ohio University branch campus in Chillicothe, six days before the midterm elections. Hawk held onto Ramaswamy’s hand and started trying to tell him everything he was dealing with, everything he wanted the Republican candidates gathered there to help him with.

Hawk, 39, told him that he was a self-employed landscaper who was having a hard time with the high cost of fuel. He told him that he was raising three young kids from two different moms, mostly on his own. He told him of his worries for his 9-year-old son, who was autistic and underweight and suffered from a two-year delay in brain development.

Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, nodded and offered some token reassurance and moved down the line, toward the arena where he would soon be appearing with President Donald Trump and Sen. Jon Husted and the rest of the Republican slate in a state that Trump had won by 11 percentage points two years ago, and which the party had dominated during the era of Trump. I had been at many Republican events in the state over that time, including a rally in an airplane hangar outside Dayton in March 2016, where a giant crowd had roared as Trump’s jet had rolled into view and where he had declared that he had come to save Ohio. “Our jobs are being sucked away,” he said then. “It’s unbelievable what’s happening.”

This event was different. Ten years had passed, and gone was the fierce bravado of Trump the conquering hero, bristling with retribution and promises. This rally was populated largely by the same sort of voters who had been particularly drawn to Trump all along , working-class Midwesterners who had not been engaged in politics before he came on the scene. But there were fewer of them — the campaign had chosen an arena that held only 2,000 — and their devotion had been subsumed by uncertainty. They were still with Trump, but they weren’t sure how to reconcile their own difficulties with the fact that he was the president during this trying time.

Take gas prices, which “are beating the hell out of me,” Hawk told me. He was trying his best not to hold them against Trump and his decision to go to war against Iran, instead faulting Congress for limiting domestic oil drilling. “The president has to go find oil in another country because Congress won’t let him find it in our country,” he said, overlooking the fact that Trump’s party has controlled both houses of Congress during his second term.

Nearby, Debbie Shock, a 57-year-old mail carrier, blamed the high fuel costs on “the stock exchange, the markets — they’re the ones that control it.” “We have oil right here in the U.S.,” she said. “Why are we buying it from other countries to begin with?”

Shock fit a profile I had gotten to know well in 2016: an Obama-Trump voter. She was loyal to Trump — “I like the man. Nobody’s perfect, you know what I mean?” — and told me she would never go back to Democrats now. Why not? I asked. “They’re covering up the child molestation,” she said. What did she mean by that? “I’ve heard stories about the sex trafficking. The Clintons are involved in it, Disney World, you know, all that.”

It would be easy to ridicule such murky talk, yet it was not much less coherent than what soon emerged on the arena stage, which was streamed on a large screen for the few hundred of us who were out on the lawn outside the arena. Trump has never been known for structured oratory, but it is hard to overstate the extent to which his digressive style has advanced since 2016, and to convey how surreal it is to experience firsthand, as the reality of what presidential communication has come to in 2026.

The rally opened with the customary introductory video of late-era Trump, an explicitly messianic framing: “God said, ‘I need someone who will be strong and courageous,’” the voice-over intones. “So God made Trump.”

Thus introduced, Trump opened his remarks with a lengthy disquisition on Husted’s body, which had newly become part of his routine. “I looked at Jon and studied his physique,” he cooed, after referring to his recent comments on Husted’s “ass.” “I studied the feet, the legs, the shoulders. I tapped him on the shoulder, and it was like hitting a piece of steel.”

When a protester inside the arena started shouting something — those of us outside couldn’t hear what — and was removed, Trump bid him good riddance: “Now he goes home and his boyfriend gets upset with him.”

There were protesters outside, too, and things were starting to heat up between them and the supporters. “What are you talking about, ‘boyfriend?’” shouted one protester, a young man. “He was just talking about Jon Husted’s ass! That’s not gay??”

A supporter in front of me, a bearded man in his 50s, stewed as he watched the protesters. “You’re going to see someone dropping like a bad habit,” he growled, as he started to move toward them, before being held back by the woman who was with him.

A moment later, Trump had moved on to Jeffrey Epstein, saying that the Democrats had protected him for years. “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” he declared. “I was the one who was totally exonerated from him. But they use it, because that’s what they do. They’re sick, weak people.”
This set off a new round of shouting outside, as cries of “pedophiles!” flew back and forth.

Suddenly, one Trump supporter near me rushed hard at a protester and knocked him to the ground, his head landing with such a thud on the blacktop that I initially thought it might be a suppressed gunshot. Dozens of officers swarmed to the spot. Cameras flashed.

A few moments later, a couple other protesters, also young men, began railing against the war against Iran. “We’re going to be the ones sent off to die for Israel,” one shouted. “‘America First,’ and you want me to die in the Middle East?”

Trump touched on the war — “they’re getting beaten very badly” — but spent far more time on his home renovations. “The White House has to be beautiful outside, it needs that exterior plaster. The bricks were falling, the stone was broken, the monuments were coming off, the beautiful windows were cracked, it looked terrible, and I fixed it very inexpensively, and now it’s more beautiful than ever,” he said. “And President Obama, who doesn’t understand cleanliness, who doesn’t understand broken cracked stone and sidewalks, who doesn’t understand that having asphalt going to your main entrance is not the right thing, we’d like to have granite and marble we’d like to have it look nice, you don’t use asphalt, you use asphalt for your streets. …”

On the ramble went. To the Haitians in nearby Springfield: “The town went from no crime to high crime,” but “they’re being moved out.” To a riff on Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his opponent Amy Acton’s mother calling her a liar, in apparent reference to Acton’s having accused her stepfather of raping her when she was 12, as he was subsequently charged with doing. The ad had met with widespread opprobrium, but Trump defended Ramaswamy. “The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar, that she is no good. … How the hell is that his problem?” To “O Canada, which has been ripping us off for years,” and Somalia, “which isn’t even a country,” and “transgender mutilization,” and his plan to rename the Strait of Hormuz for himself.

Finally, Trump ceded the stage to Husted and Ramaswamy. But by then, the lawn had emptied out as people drifted home, Jacob Hawk among them. A vendor was shouting out discount prices on his MAGA merchandise. “$10 special on hats! All the hats are $10! These are normally $25 hats. That’s a good hat for $10.”

The next day, the full Republican slate of statewide candidates appeared, sans Trump, at a small pep rally inside a former Delphi auto-parts factory in Vandalia, outside Dayton. It is an enormous building that employed more than 100 prior to its closing in 2009 and is now being used as a warehouse by a company that sells air conditioners, employing only 10 or so; Delphi announcements still remained on the bulletin boards, adding a ghostly feel.

The setting was an unintentional reminder of what Ohio has been through. Between 2000 and 2025, the state lost 300,000 manufacturing jobs, a devastation that had made it highly susceptible to Trump’s message in 2016. But Republicans have been in charge of the state since 2010, and so it was the task of the candidates gathered there, with an audience of just a few dozen, to cast the state as being on an upswing. Complicating this challenge is the fact that so much of the state’s recent growth has been concentrated in the Columbus area: countless data centers, defense contractor Anduril, a massive Intel plant under construction.

The bigger challenge, though, was the nationwide pall that hung over the event: the reality of stubbornly high inflation and high gas prices, the latter a direct consequence of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. He had stood against costly foreign entanglements when he ran in 2016, in opposition to his party’s recent record, and carried that same banner again in 2024. But another aspect of his political persona had prevailed: a heedless swagger that, in this case, had been fanned by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It had led him into this drawn-out conflict that has already cost U.S. taxpayers more than $47 billion.

And it had left a long row of Republican candidates standing in this giant building stacked high with made-in-China air conditioners all but pleading the small assemblage to save them from the political climate. “You can’t give up,” Husted said. “This is a Republican state, and the only way Democrats can win is if Republicans don’t vote.”

Five days later, I was in York County, Pennsylvania, which Trump had won by 25 points in 2024, and which was home to one of four Republican-held House districts targeted by Democrats. I chose to go to a precinct on the outskirts of York, thinking it would offer a diverse cross-section, in between more Democratic York proper and more Republican rural areas. But over 90 minutes of conversations, I didn’t encounter a Republican voter until I was about to call it a day.

The first person I spoke with, Bill, a 52-year-old state government employee who asked that I not use his last name for fear of losing his job, had voted for Trump three times. He hardly considered himself MAGA but was drawn in 2016 to Trump’s “drain the swamp” rhetoric and his disavowal of the war in Iraq. He voted for him again in 2020 and 2024 because he didn’t think much of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris.

But on this day, Bill was coming to vote against his Republican representative, Scott Perry, because he was too “Trump adjacent.” Bill had finally had enough of Trump, especially when it came to all the revelations of self-dealing involving his family and cronies. “I will not be falling for him again,” he told me. “Drain the swamp, no wars. … It was all a lie.”

He said he couldn’t understand how Trump had gone from America First to seemingly letting the country’s foreign policy be dictated by Israel. He said that he was voting for the Democrats mainly just for the sake of “gridlock,” as deliberate blockage. “Someone’s got to stop this,” he said. “It’s getting out of control.”
Each Democratic voter I spoke with after that was coming with their own motivation for voting against the Republican slate, like the cast of “Murder on the Orient Express.”

For Annie (who also asked that I not use her last name), it was for Trump’s social-welfare cuts, which had cost her and her disabled husband $300 per month in SNAP benefits and nearly cost them their Medicaid coverage.
For Desiree Edmonds, an elementary school teacher, it was high inflation, which was translating into anxiety among the working-class children in her classroom.
For Mark Castillo, a 19-year-old ironworker, it was for the sky-high cost of diesel.
For Jacqueline Jimenez, a native Puerto Rican who worked as a home-health aide, it was for the excessive harshness of ICE arrests.

For Shiri Kramer, a warehouse worker, it was for the general meanness emanating from the administration, which made her think of her grandfather, a Jewish American who had extended mercy to German POWs during World War II. “My grandfather would be writhing right now,” she said. “Nothing happening in our country is OK.”

By night’s end, Republicans had lost this Pennsylvania district by 10 points, as well as the other three in the state and more than 40 nationwide. They had lost at least seven Senate seats, even in states where Democrats hadn’t prevailed in decades — Kansas, Texas, South Carolina. Incredibly, even Mississippi was on the verge. In Ohio, Republicans lost the race for Senate and governor — only one of the seven statewide candidates on stage at the warehouse emerged a victor — as well as two Republican-held House seats, a stark reversal in a state that had seemed to be trending away from Democrats for good. In all, Democrats flipped five governorships and up to 12 state legislative chambers. The Democratic popular-vote margin in congressional races nationwide was 13 percentage points — nearly double the Republican margin in their own wave years of 2010 and 1994, and approaching the scale of the historic Democratic rout in the post-Watergate election of 1974.

The particularly stunning loss of the South Carolina seat brought to mind a warning issued in May 2016 by Lindsey Graham, whose death this July left the seat vacant. “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed…….and we will deserve it,” Graham tweeted in 2016. For years, the Republican Party had avoided the catastrophic reckoning he warned of — through Trump’s narrow win in 2016, through the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol , through Biden’s fateful insistence on running for reelection at age 81 in 2024. Along the way, much of the party, including Graham himself, had accommodated itself to Trump. One way of looking at the 2026 results was that the warning had finally come true. The reckoning had been delayed by a decade, but it had gathered more force over time, like a boulder rolling downhill.
There was a hint of such a reckoning in the words that Bill, the three-time Trump voter, left me with in York. After he returned from voting, he bade me farewell with a parting regret.
“You see what’s going on,” he said, “and you’re like, ‘What the hell did I do?’”
The post On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm Debacle appeared first on ProPublica .

items.title: Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stands on the shoulders of Stacey Abrams, Charlotta Bass and countless other Black women who dreamed
items.abstract: For generations, Black women have been asked to save a democracy that would not save them, carrying entire movements on their backs. Now a Black woman has been elected to govern Georgia.
paras: There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers.
Georgia remembers.
The auction blocks . The cotton fields . The lynching trees . The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves.
And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected Georgia’s first Black woman governor . The first Black woman elected governor of any American state.
Bottoms has traced her ancestry back five generations to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia.
An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil. A descendant elected to govern it.
The same earth. An entirely different claim to power. How many women had to believe in a future they would never live to see?

Bottoms’s victory represents the paradox of Black political advancement amid racial violence and the often-unrecognized labor of women who build futures they may never inhabit. Ultimately, Bottoms’ victory reflects both extraordinary progress and the unfinished work of American democracy.
The children who deserved a future
I keep thinking about the little children.

Between 1979 and 1981, Atlanta was terrorized by the disappearances and murders of Black children and young adults. Mothers pleaded for answers. Families lived in a city where childhood itself had become dangerous.

The murders unfolded just years after Maynard Jackson’s historic 1973 election as Atlanta’s first Black mayor. His victory announced a new era of Black political power. Yet that power could not shield the city’s most vulnerable children. Suspicions of Ku Klux Klan involvement circulated , although the Klan’s responsibility was never established.
That distinction matters. So does the fear.

Bottoms was born in 1970 . She was 9 when the murders began. She grew up in the same Atlanta where Black parents searched desperately for their missing children. She belonged to the generation whose futures were being stolen. And now she is preparing to lead the entire state.
What a terrible, beautiful, complicated thing.
Those murdered children were not symbols waiting to become useful to history. They were sons and daughters who deserved the ordinary miracle of growing older. They deserved a future.

Bottoms later occupied the mayor’s office that Jackson first opened to Black leadership. Now she is preparing to occupy the governor’s mansion. History has not erased its cruelty. But it has delivered an astonishing answer.
And this victory does not belong to Bottoms alone.
The woman who sowed the seeds
This victory belongs, in no small measure, to democracy advocate, legislator and lawyer Stacey Abrams . Perhaps those who recognize what Abrams made possible have sent her flowers.

Abrams ran for Georgia governor in 2018 and 2022. She lost both races . But through the New Georgia Project and Fair Fight , organizations focused on engaging voters and protecting voting rights, she helped build an electorate that could imagine Georgia differently. She registered voters, challenged barriers to participation , and refused to accept that the South’s political future was fixed.

And now another Black woman has won the office Abrams twice sought, in the third gubernatorial race in a row headed by a Black Democratic woman . There is something biblical about the path Abrams steadfastly cleared. I think of Moses, guiding his people toward the Promised Land but never entering it himself.

Abrams’ journey is not over. Nor should her accomplishments be measured by another woman’s victory. But I believe there is sacred work in preparing a future you may never personally enjoy. Some people plant trees. Some people sit in their shade. Stacey Abrams planted. Bottoms is standing beneath the branches.
And as a scholar of Black media history , I can reach even further back, to another woman who understood the audacity of claiming political power: Charlotta Bass .
In 1952, Bass became the first Black woman nominated for vice president of the United States, running on the Progressive Party ticket.
The future Charlotta dared to imagine
Before the Voting Rights Act in 1965, before the March on Washington in 1963, before Jackson was elected mayor in 1973 and before Abrams or Bottoms drew their first breaths, there was Bass.

A Black newspaper publisher who confronted segregation, police brutality and white supremacist violence in her four-decade ownership of The California Eagle , Bass understood that political power was about more than winning office. It was about who had the right to imagine themselves in one.

Bass ran when a Black woman entering the White House seemed almost unimaginable. Almost. But not to her. I imagine she would have loved this election. And I suspect she would have had pointed questions for Gov.-elect Bottoms.
What will you do for the poor? The disenfranchised? How will you protect the vote that brought you here?

History-making is not the same as justice-making, and representation matters. The true measure of Bottoms’ victory will be whether Georgians experience the more just state she promised to bring about .
The work beyond the win

For generations, Black women have been asked to save a democracy that would not save them. We have carried clipboards, protest signs and entire movements on our backs. We have been told to wait. To be patient. To be grateful.
And now a Black woman has been elected to govern Georgia.

The children have not returned. The past has not been undone. But something has shifted. Charlotta dreamed it. Stacey helped build it. Keisha has won it. And somewhere, another little Black girl is watching. She may not understand the history. She may only know that the governor-elect looks like her. For now, that is enough to begin a dream.
And history has taught us what can happen when a Black girl begins to dream.
